questions.question: Which Mamluk market forms a monumental approach toward Al-Aqsa?
questions.explanation: Souq al-Qattanin is a vaulted Mamluk market whose eastern gate opens toward the Haram al-Sharif/Al-Aqsa compound.
questions.source_note: Muslim Quarter §4–5; Museum With No Frontiers, Suq al-Qattanin

questions.question: Under which governor was Souq al-Qattanin completed in 1336–1337?
questions.explanation: The market and associated complex were completed under the Mamluk governor Tankiz al-Nasiri in 737 AH/1336–1337 CE.
questions.source_note: Muslim Quarter §2 and §5; Museum With No Frontiers

questions.question: Which architectural detail should visitors look for at the Qattanin entrance?
options: Alternating stone colours and inscription bands
questions.explanation: The monumental entrance uses coloured stonework, carving and inscription bands typical of prestigious Mamluk portals.
questions.source_note: Muslim Quarter §5 and §9; Jerusalem Studies, Khan Tankaz

questions.question: Why is the Muslim Quarter described as more than an archaeological district?
options: It is a lived neighbourhood of homes, schools, worship and trade
questions.explanation: Its heritage includes continuing residential, educational, religious and commercial life, not monuments alone.

questions.question: Which Christian devotional route crosses part of the quarter?
questions.explanation: The Via Dolorosa passes through the quarter, adding a Christian pilgrimage route to its overlapping urban histories.

questions.question: Which arrangement regulates shared responsibilities at the Church of the Holy Sepulchre?
questions.explanation: Several Christian communities share spaces and responsibilities under the historic Status Quo arrangements.

questions.question: In which year was Constantine's Holy Sepulchre complex dedicated?
questions.explanation: The Constantinian church was dedicated in 335 CE over a site identified in Christian tradition with Calvary and the tomb.
questions.source_note: Christian Quarter §2; Oxford Reference, Church of the Holy Sepulchre

questions.question: What major architectural phase was dedicated in 1149?
options: The Crusader rebuilding of the Holy Sepulchre
questions.explanation: Crusader builders unified major sacred spaces into much of the Romanesque church form visible today.
questions.source_note: Christian Quarter §2; JSAH Crusader reconstruction study

questions.question: What should visitors notice on the church's entrance façade?
questions.explanation: The entrance has paired Crusader-period Romanesque portals; one remains sealed while the other is used.

questions.question: Why can circulation inside the church change without notice?
options: Active services and processions share the building
Visitors must follow a fixed museum tour
questions.explanation: It is a living, shared place of worship, so ceremonies and processions may temporarily alter visitor movement.

questions.question: Which craft became a distinctive Armenian contribution to modern Jerusalem?
questions.explanation: Armenian artists arriving from 1919 developed a distinctive Jerusalem school of painted tile and pottery.
questions.source_note: Armenian Quarter §2 and §5; Tel Aviv University ceramics history

questions.question: When did the Armenian Patriarchate establish its Jerusalem printing press?
questions.explanation: The printing press was founded in 1833 and became an important centre of Armenian-language publishing.
questions.source_note: Armenian Quarter §2 and §5; St James Printing House research

questions.question: Much of the present Cathedral of St James dates to which period?
questions.explanation: Much of the current cathedral took shape during the twelfth century while preserving earlier traditions and fabric.

questions.question: What was the nineteenth-century building now used by the Armenian Museum originally built for?
questions.explanation: It was built in the 1850s as a pilgrim guesthouse and later served community and refugee needs before becoming a museum.
questions.source_note: Armenian Quarter §2; Associated Press museum report

questions.question: Which detail best helps identify the Armenian Quarter in the street?
options: Blue-and-white ceramic plaques and Armenian script
questions.explanation: Armenian inscriptions, carved cross-stones and hand-painted ceramic plaques mark the community landscape.

questions.question: With which wider region was the historic Maghariba Quarter connected?
questions.explanation: The quarter served communities and pilgrims connected with North Africa and the wider Maghreb.

questions.question: Which year is associated with the Ayyubid endowment for Maghrebi residents and pilgrims?
questions.explanation: Historical accounts associate the charitable endowment with 1193 CE, soon after Salah al-Din restored Muslim rule.

questions.question: What happened to most of the quarter on 10–11 June 1967?
options: It was demolished and residents were displaced
It was enclosed by a new medieval wall
It was moved outside the Old City
questions.explanation: Most of the built fabric was demolished and residents were displaced, leaving a radically changed urban setting.
questions.source_note: Maghariba Quarter §2 and §5; UNESCO and PASSIA documentation

questions.question: What is essential for understanding the neighbourhood that no longer survives intact?
options: Historic photographs, waqf records and testimony
questions.explanation: Archival images, records and attributed family testimony help reconstruct the erased lanes and social fabric.

questions.question: Which visitor method best reads this site responsibly?
options: Assume the present plaza is unchanged since antiquity
Compare the current space with a dated historical view
questions.explanation: A dated comparison reveals the sharp change in scale and prevents the modern plaza from being mistaken for an unchanged ancient space.

questions.question: When did prominent Jerusalem families expand housing in Sheikh Jarrah outside the walls?
questions.explanation: Prominent Palestinian families built residences there during Jerusalem's late nineteenth-century expansion.

questions.question: When was the Isaf al-Nashashibi house completed?
questions.explanation: The house was completed in 1922 and its design is attributed to architect Spiro Khouri.

questions.question: How many housing units do UN records note as completed in 1956?
questions.explanation: UN documentation records completion of 28 units connected with an arrangement for 28 refugee families.
questions.source_note: Sheikh Jarrah §2 and §5; United Nations records

questions.question: Which features express the neighbourhood's villa heritage?
options: Stone arches, deep windows, tiled roofs and gardens
questions.explanation: Late Ottoman and Mandate-era villas use Jerusalem stone, arched openings, verandas, tiled roofs and planted gardens.

questions.question: Why must current property cases not be answered from the static heritage summary?
options: Legal outcomes and conditions can change
questions.explanation: Current legal facts are time-sensitive and require up-to-date authoritative sources; architectural history cannot determine them.

questions.question: Which feature is central to Silwan's historic landscape?
questions.explanation: Ain Silwan connects water, settlement, cultivation and the neighbourhood's living heritage.

questions.question: Which medieval geographer described the spring and cultivated landscape below Jerusalem?
questions.explanation: The tenth-century geographer al-Muqaddasi described Jerusalem's water and cultivated landscape.

questions.question: What do Silwan's retaining walls and stacked roofs help visitors understand?
questions.explanation: Homes, paths and terraces respond to a steep valley-side landscape that is best read vertically.

questions.question: Why should archaeology and present community life not be conflated?
options: Only one of them is real
They are different evidence layers sharing the same landscape
questions.explanation: Ancient remains and contemporary Palestinian life overlap spatially but answer different historical and social questions.

questions.question: Which practical advice fits Silwan's terrain?
options: Wear shoes with grip and avoid unmarked shortcuts
questions.explanation: The slopes and paths can be steep and uneven, so stable footwear and locally verified routes are important.

questions.question: What can the Mount of Olives viewpoint help visitors read?
options: The relation of walls, valleys and eastern ridge
questions.explanation: The panorama shows the physical relationship among the Old City walls, Kidron Valley and eastern ridge.

questions.question: Which valley separates the Mount of Olives from the Old City?
questions.explanation: The Kidron Valley lies between the eastern Old City wall and the Mount of Olives ridge.
questions.source_note: At-Tur §5; Custody of the Holy Land

questions.question: When was the present Church of All Nations consecrated?
questions.explanation: The present church at Gethsemane, designed by Antonio Barluzzi above earlier remains, was consecrated in 1924.
questions.source_note: At-Tur §2 and §5; Custody of the Holy Land

questions.question: What creates the church's solemn visual atmosphere?
options: Dark blue vaults and subdued light
questions.explanation: Its dark blue vaulting and controlled light contrast with the bright valley outside and support a devotional atmosphere.

questions.question: Which statement best respects the ridge's identity?
options: It is only a pilgrimage viewpoint
It is both a sacred landscape and a living Palestinian neighbourhood
All tomb identifications are archaeologically certain
questions.explanation: Homes, schools, hospitals and local commerce coexist with shrines, cemeteries and viewpoints.

questions.question: The visible monumental façade of Bab al-Amud belongs mainly to which period?
questions.explanation: The present façade was built in 1537–1540 as part of Sultan Suleiman's Ottoman walls, above earlier remains.

questions.question: What is the likely origin of the Arabic name Bab al-Amud, “Gate of the Column”?
options: A column shown in the Roman plaza
questions.explanation: The sixth-century Madaba map shows a column in the inner Roman plaza, remembered in the Arabic name.
questions.source_note: Bab al-Amud §2 and §3; University of Michigan gate record

questions.question: During whose reign was the earlier Roman gate complex built?
questions.explanation: The Roman gate complex dates to the reign of Hadrian, when the city was refounded as Aelia Capitolina.
questions.source_note: Bab al-Amud §2; University of Michigan gate record

questions.question: Why does the gate passage turn instead of running straight through?
options: To create a defensive bent entrance
To make room for a railway
questions.explanation: The bent-axis passage controls movement and prevents a direct approach through the fortification.

questions.question: Which market route continues south after entering the gate?
questions.explanation: Khan al-Zeit carries the route into the Old City through a roofed commercial street.
